title: Adaptive Hypermedia
extended_summary:
This paper is a broad state-of-the-art review of adaptive hypermedia research as it stood around the year 2000. It addresses the problem that traditional hypermedia systems present the same content and links to all users, which is inadequate for diverse audiences with different goals, knowledge, interests, abilities, and contexts of use. The paper’s purpose is not to report a single empirical study, but to organize the field, summarize major systems and techniques, and identify future research directions.

The paper reviews adaptive hypermedia across several application areas, especially educational hypermedia, online information systems, information retrieval, and personalized information spaces. It describes how systems model user goals, knowledge, interests, preferences, individual traits, and environment factors such as location and platform. It also classifies adaptation techniques into content adaptation and navigation support, including link hiding, sorting, annotation, direct guidance, and adaptive link generation. The review discusses developments such as Web-based adaptive courseware, adaptive encyclopedias, virtual museum guides, e-commerce personalization, and performance support systems.

The paper does not study a K-12 population or a specific intervention in schools. Instead, it argues that adaptive hypermedia had matured by 2000 and was expanding toward new application areas, new AI methods, mobile devices, and component-based architectures. Its main conclusion is that adaptive hypermedia is moving beyond static one-size-fits-all systems toward more context-sensitive, user-modeled, and dynamically generated support, with especially promising future directions in natural language generation, non-symbolic AI, open-corpus systems, and reusable development frameworks.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative state-of-the-art review and forecast paper, not an empirical study with a clearly identifiable evaluation design. It does not report original outcomes, effect sizes, or a systematic evidence synthesis.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not demonstrate measured impact on learner outcomes, teacher workload, or equity; it mainly surveys the field and proposes future directions. No actionable effect size or intervention result is reported.

interventions.use_case: Review of adaptive hypermedia systems that personalize educational content, navigation, and presentation based on learner models (e.g., knowledge, goals, preferences, learning style) in Web-based education.
